analysis.one_liner: Taxes big investment funds that buy single-family homes, forcing them to sell down their portfolios and funding down-payment help for homebuyers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from December 2023 until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tax large investment firms — hedge funds, private equity, and real estate investment trusts that pool investor money — that buy and hold single-family homes. New purchases by firms with $50 million or more in assets would face a tax of 50% of the home's value, and existing holdings would be taxed $50,000 per home per year under a schedule that forces firms to sell down nearly their entire portfolios over about a decade. The money raised would go into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund to help families buy homes, with priority given to buyers of homes the firms are forced to sell [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: First-time homebuyers would benefit twice: large investor owners would be pushed to sell homes onto the market (sales to ordinary buyers would be prioritized through the grant program), and the tax revenue would fund a new Housing Downpayment Trust Fund, with HUD grants to state housing finance agencies to help families cover down payments, with priority given to families buying homes sold off by the taxed investors [S2] [S3]. Renters in neighborhoods dominated by investor-owned rentals could also benefit if more homes shift to owner-occupants [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Pressures large investors out of the single-family home market: a 50% tax on each newly acquired home makes further bulk buying economically prohibitive for firms with $50 million or more in assets, and a $50,000-per-home annual tax forces existing portfolios down by at least 10% each year until, for hedge fund taxpayers, they are essentially eliminated after nine years
Channels the tax revenue into a Housing Downpayment Trust Fund, which HUD would use to grant money to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance to families buying homes

Steers homes toward ordinary buyers: the forced sell-down rules only count sales to individual buyers who own no other home, and families buying a home from a taxed investor get priority for down-payment assistance grants

analysis.who_pays: Investment entities that pool investor money and hold $50 million or more in assets — hedge funds, private equity funds, and real estate investment trusts — would pay a 50% tax on every single-family home they newly buy, and a $50,000-per-home annual tax that forces them to sell off their existing portfolios almost entirely within ten years. Entities managing pooled funds below $50 million would keep a allowance of 50 homes before the tax applies. A $20,000 penalty applies for failing to report required ownership and sale information [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax only reaches entities that manage pooled investor money with $50 million or more in assets; large landlords structured as ordinary corporations or family partnerships outside that definition face no forced sell-down at all (only a 50-home allowance), so much investor ownership could escape the bill entirely

A 50% tax on investor purchases of newly built or existing homes could shrink a source of demand that some economists argue supports home construction and neighborhood home values, though the bill exempts entities primarily engaged in construction or rehabilitation

Forcing large portfolios to be sold within roughly ten years could produce rushed sales, and rental costs could rise in the interim if owners facing the annual tax raise rents or let properties deteriorate while divesting
A sale does not count toward the sell-down requirement if the buyer is a business or an individual who owns any other home, which narrows the pool of qualifying buyers and could slow divestiture

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and growing driver of housing costs — large investor ownership of single-family homes — and pairs the pressure to divest with down-payment help for the buyers who would absorb those homes, a coherent design. Its main weakness is that it only covers investment entities pooling investor money with $50 million or more in assets, leaving many large landlords outside its reach, and its divestiture schedule could create disruption for tenants during the transition. Since it never became law, none of these tradeoffs were ever tested legislatively.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day
The committee took no further action on the bill; the complete action history shows only the introduction and the referral, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and any reintroduction in a new Congress would have to start over

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutional investors in single-family rental homes are better off: no tax was ever created, so they continued acquiring homes through the end of the 118th Congress without new cost. No down-payment assistance fund was created either, so aspiring homebuyers gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee on December 5, 2023

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: As chair of the Senate Finance Committee, the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat with no further action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: As Senate Majority Leader in the 118th Congress, never brought the bill to the floor; no Senate action is recorded after the committee referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by one Democrat and cosponsored only by two other Democrats, with no Republican support in evidence; it never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (hedge funds, private equity, REITs)
industries.note: These firms profit by buying homes that might otherwise go to owner-occupants and renting them out; the bill's 50% purchase tax and forced ten-year sell-down would directly reduce that business. In this bill the industry's interest runs squarely against ordinary buyers.

Organizations primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating single-family homes are explicitly excluded from the tax, so homebuilders' business of selling new homes to investors is preserved. Firms that own rental portfolios alongside building operations would still face the sell-down on the ownership side.
The bill directs the new trust fund to HUD grants to these agencies to run down-payment assistance programs, a new funding stream, though it only exists if the tax raises revenue first.

industries.industry: Small and mid-size landlords owning more than 50 homes
industries.note: Investment funds below the $50 million threshold keep a 50-home allowance before any tax, while smaller landlords must still sell only to buyers who do not own other homes for their sales to count toward the limit — a rule that narrows their buyer pool.
